units.text: Let's trace how a bucket setting becomes a compliance decision. Config records the state of supported resources you select. A rule checks the recorded state. That tells you whether it meets the rule, not whether the setting change was prevented.
A noncompliant outcome can lead to scoped remediation if you configure it. Verify recording in the intended account and Region, then confirm the changed resource state after any corrective action.

The bucket appears at two times. The configuration items show the state recorded at each time, including the changed public-access-block settings. Find the first recorded difference before asking who made the change.

The resource timeline is only as complete as the recording scope and available history. Check which resources were selected and where recording was active. It is not a complete record of A P I activity.
Config shows the bucket's recorded configuration before and after the change. Use that to establish what changed and when it appeared in the configuration history.

CloudTrail can show the recorded A P I operation, identity, time and outcome. Join it to the Config record by resource and timing. One answers what changed; the other can help explain who or what made the call.
Use a managed rule when A W S already provides the check you need. For custom evaluation, choose Guard for suitable policy-as-code conditions or Lambda when the rule needs custom processing.
Choose a supported trigger based on whether you need evaluation after a relevant configuration change or on a schedule. A failed rule evaluates compliance; it doesn't by itself stop the change.
Detective evaluation looks at existing resources and reports compliance based on the configured trigger. In this bucket example, it evaluates the configuration that is already in place.

Proactive evaluation can test supported proposed properties before deployment. Use the result in an authorized deployment control if it needs to block a change. The evaluation alone does not block or remediate it.

A rule reports noncompliance. A Systems Manager Automation runbook can make a scoped change with its configured role. Choose manual approval for a sensitive change rather than making every response automatic.
A runbook reporting success is not the exit test. Verify the intended bucket setting, confirm required access still works, and make sure the relevant rule reevaluates the resource as intended.

Let's investigate an event without expecting one log to answer everything. CloudTrail can identify a recorded A P I call. Flow logs describe network traffic metadata, not packet contents. Resolver logs answer a D N S question, while load balancer access logs can provide request and response details.

For the suspicious access example, compare time, resource and relevant addresses across available sources. If two records line up, use the association to guide investigation, not as proof that you already know the full cause.

We'll trace how a security signal reaches an analyst. GuardDuty analyzes supported activity and produces a finding when it detects a potential issue. The finding can be routed to an investigation or response workflow; it's not itself proof of compromise.

Check the relevant accounts and Regions first, then verify the protection plans needed by the workloads. Enabling foundational detection does not automatically prove every optional data source is covered.

Foundational detection analyzes management events, network flow data and supported Route 53 Resolver D N S data from independent service streams. You don't need to create your own matching log destinations for those streams. Coverage still depends on what data is available to GuardDuty.

If the concern is S three object activity, E K S, database login activity, Lambda networking or malware, choose the relevant protection plan and eligible resources. These plans extend coverage beyond foundational activity; one plan doesn't stand in for all the others.

A GuardDuty finding can match an EventBridge rule and notify the response owner. Validate the signal and the affected resource before taking action. The workflow should make responsibility explicit rather than leaving the alert unowned.

For approved containment, choose the smallest change that addresses the confirmed issue. Verify the intended result, record the evidence and keep the owner informed. A missed validation can cause more disruption than the original signal.

A delegated administrator can manage member accounts in each enabled Region. Follow each account into its intended Region and verify coverage there. Seeing an account in one Region is not proof it is protected in every other Region.
Review auto-enable settings for new accounts and check the regions you actually need. A cross-Region dashboard is a way to view results, not a way to turn on a detector in those Regions.

Let's take a finding and ask which activity is related. Detective builds a behavior graph from supported sources, including management events, flow data and GuardDuty findings. Optional sources can add context when enabled. Coverage depends on what the graph received.

An analyst can compare related identities, resources and timelines. Use that to test a hypothesis against available evidence. A relationship in the graph doesn't by itself justify declaring compromise.
Open the finding and check the affected identity and resource in the relevant time range. Compare the network and A P I evidence before concluding that nearby activity has the same cause.

The analyst tests whether the activity is unusual for the identity and consistent with other evidence. If a response is justified, have the owner approve and verify a scoped action. Keep the investigation trace along with the result.

Macie can inventory supported S three buckets and analyze eligible objects for sensitive data. Inventory describes what is there; it doesn't mean every object's contents were scanned. Choose automated discovery or a scoped job according to your coverage need.
Unsupported storage classes or formats and inaccessible encryption keys can leave content unexamined. Macie reports findings; it doesn't automatically encrypt the objects or repair bucket access.

Follow a supported object into sensitive data discovery. Managed or custom identifiers find the kinds of content you specify. A sensitive data finding is about detected object contents; a bucket policy finding is about the bucket itself.

Review the affected bucket, key and finding type with an authorized analyst. Preserve the minimum evidence needed. The goal is to confirm and limit exposure, not to repeat the sensitive value in tickets or reports.

Check which buckets, storage classes, formats and objects are eligible. Choose the right identifiers and review any allow list. A narrow scope can be useful, but the absence of a finding only speaks to what you actually examined.

Use the finding's data and access context to choose a scoped fix, such as tightening bucket access. Verify the authorized readers still have the access they need, and check the relevant security state after applying it.
